8.0.s.en: (3) The death of the scoffing officer

8.0.0.en: Elisha still appreciated the kindness of the Shunammite woman who had hosted him in her house. After giving her a son and then raising him from the dead, he now grants her a favor by telling her of a famine that would come upon the land of Canaan for seven years. He advised her to sojourn in another country. Most likely her husband had died, so she had to lead her household, that is, her son and her servants, and go to a place where there was no famine.

8.0.1.en: It should be noted that this famine prevailed over the whole land of Canaan and is different from the limited famine that occurred in Samaria when the Arameans besieged it. The problem was greater and would last seven years, so God took care to provide for His children during it. Perhaps this was a discipline from God, so that His people would repent and turn back from the worship of idols.

8.0.2.en: Elisha's concern to advise the Shunammite to sojourn abroad was necessary, because the Shunammite was most likely a widow and wealthy, and in famines there is disorder, plundering of property and killing. Because of her wealth, the Shunammite was exposed to being killed and having her possessions plundered.

8.0.3.en: God's gifts to His special children are many, and He cares for them more than for the rest of people, so that they may rely on Him and devote themselves to loving Him. So do not worry about tomorrow, and trust that God will provide for it for you; live today with God in prayers and meditations, and you will enjoy Him, for He loves you.

8.1.0.en: The Shunammite obeyed Elisha's command, because she believed the word of God spoken through His prophet, and she went to the land of the Philistines, which lies south of the land of the Jews and was not struck by the famine. That is why Elisha agreed that she should sojourn there.

8.2.0.en: When the seven years ended, the woman returned to her homeland from the land of the Philistines, where she had taken refuge during the famine, but she was surprised to find that others had taken possession of her property, the house and the field. So she went to the king to complain.

8.3.0.en: At that time the king had summoned Gehazi, Elisha's servant, and asked him to tell him all the miracles that had been done by Elisha. Two things are understood from this:

8.3.1.en: 1- That the king knew that the power of God was in Elisha, so he showed interest in hearing the stories of his miracles, even though he did not carry out Elisha's teachings and still worshiped idols and did not obey God's commandments. He represents the person who wants to know information about God but does not submit to it.

8.3.2.en: 2- That Gehazi was near the king. Either the king had summoned him before the leprosy of Naaman came upon him, that is, before he was struck with leprosy, or he had tried to honor him after his bringing the good news of the Aramean camp and the spoil. It appears from the stories of Gehazi that he benefited from being Elisha's disciple, for he now teaches and proclaims the word of God.

8.4.0.en: The wonderful providence of God appears here. He made the king summon Gehazi to hear from him the miracles of Elisha; then Gehazi tells some of the miracles, and the king's heart is drawn to love Elisha and his works; then he tells the story of the Shunammite and the raising of her son; then God allows the Shunammite to come to the king at that very time to appeal to him to rescue her and restore to her her land and the property taken from her, which people had seized during the seven years of her absence. The king was eager for the story and attached to it, and his attachment grew because, when the Shunammite woman came in to cry to the king to rescue her, Gehazi said to the king, "This is the woman I am telling you about, and this is her son, who died and whom Elisha raised." The king rejoiced and became eager to know more details from the woman of the story, and ready to grant any request she made, because of his admiration for her faith, her love and her generosity.

8.5.0.en: The king asked the woman to tell him her story with Elisha, and she related to him greater details, which increased his admiration for her and for Elisha. When he heard her problem and the seizure of her land, he was ready to fulfill all her requests, so he hurried to restore her rights and gave her one of his servants, one of the eunuchs who worked for him, to restore to her, by the king's command, her land and all her property, and even all the produce that the land had yielded during the seven years, or its equivalent in silver and gold. From this we see several things:

8.5.1.en: 1- God gave the woman more than she asked: she asked for the land, and God gives her the produce as well for the whole seven years.

8.5.2.en: 2- The king is an instrument in God's hand, with which He does what He wills for the good of His children (Prov 21:1).

8.5.3.en: 3- The land did produce during the famine, but its yield was meager and not enough for the people's food. This means that the Shunammite was exposed to people attacking her to take the produce of her land and to harm her, and God rescued her by her sojourn in Philistia.

8.5.4.en: (2) Hazael seizes the throne of Aram (vv. 7-15)

8.5.5.en: 7- And Elisha came to Damascus; and Benhadad the king of Syria was sick; and it was told him, saying, The man of God is come hither. 8- And the king said unto Hazael, Take a present in thine hand, and go, meet the man of God, and enquire of the LORD by him, saying, Shall I recover of this disease? 9- So Hazael went to meet him, and took a present with him, even of every good thing of Damascus, forty camels' burden, and came and stood before him, and said, Thy son Benhadad king of Syria hath sent me to thee, saying, Shall I recover of this disease? 10- And Elisha said unto him, Go, say unto him, Thou mayest certainly recover: howbeit the LORD hath shewed me that he shall surely die.

8.5.6.en: 11- And he settled his countenance stedfastly, until he was ashamed: and the man of God wept. 12- And Hazael said, Why weepeth my lord? And he answered, Because I know the evil that thou wilt do unto the children of Israel: their strong holds wilt thou set on fire, and their young men wilt thou slay with the sword, and wilt dash their children, and rip up their women with child. 13- And Hazael said, But what, is thy servant a dog, that he should do this great thing? And Elisha answered, The LORD hath shewed me that thou shalt be king over Syria. 14- So he departed from Elisha, and came to his master; who said to him, What said Elisha to thee? And he answered, He told me that thou shouldest surely recover. 15- And it came to pass on the morrow, that he took a thick cloth, and dipped it in water, and spread it on his face, so that he died: and Hazael reigned in his stead.

8.6.0.en: Elisha went to Damascus to fulfill what God had commanded Elijah in (1 Kgs 19:15), which was to anoint Hazael king over Aram. Although he did not anoint him, he declared to him that he would be king, because Hazael would become a Gentile king and persecute the people of God, so Elisha's coming was to meet Hazael and warn him of what he would do. God warns all people, righteous and wicked, so that all are without excuse before Him if they do evil, and so that He may give everyone an opportunity to repent.

8.6.1.en: Elisha the man of God was openly visible and not hidden, so when he reached Damascus, King Benhadad learned of his arrival. Benhadad was a general name for the kings of Aram, and it means "worshiper of the sun." This Benhadad was the one who sent Naaman to Elisha to be healed, and he was also the one who besieged Samaria, so he was wicked; yet he knew the power of Elisha, and because he was sick and weak, he longed for the man of God to heal him, or at least to prophesy to him of recovery.

8.7.0.en: King Benhadad commanded one of his commanders, Hazael, to take a present and go to welcome Elisha and ask him to inquire of the Lord whether he, that is, Benhadad, would recover from his illness and regain his health. Perhaps Benhadad wanted by this present to honor Elisha so that he would prophesy his recovery, and forgot that this was the man of God, who speaks only the word of God and is not swayed by gifts, since he had not accepted the gifts of Naaman, whom he healed.

8.7.1.en: It is remarkable that Benhadad, the pagan king, inquires of God by means of His prophet Elisha, while Ahaziah king of Israel inquired of Baal-zebub to prophesy his recovery to him; therefore the divine sentence of death came upon him, and Ahaziah died in the days of Elijah (2 Kgs 1:2).

8.8.0.en: Hazael carried out King Benhadad's command. He gathered of all the good things for which Damascus is famous, put them on forty camels, and came to Elisha, delivering to him the king's message and asking him to tell him whether he, that is, Benhadad, would recover from his illness or not.

8.8.1.en: The sending of this great present, carried on forty camels, means the following:

8.8.2.en: 1- The wealth and power of King Benhadad.

8.8.3.en: 2- His esteem for Elisha, especially since he called him father and considered him a father, saying "thy son Benhadad," as the kings of Israel call him. This is a great honor to the prophet of God, but unfortunately it was not accompanied by faith in God and a change of his conduct, for he still worshiped idols, and even compelled Naaman, the commander of his army, to share in this worship.

8.9.0.en: Elisha told Hazael God's answer to Benhadad's question about his recovery: that God tells him he will recover. But Elisha completed his words, saying that Benhadad would die, not from the illness but for another reason, which we shall learn from the following verses, for Hazael would kill him (v. 15).

8.10.0.en: After Elisha told Hazael God's answer, Elisha looked at Hazael with a strong and searching gaze and continued looking at him for a while. During this Hazael felt the power of the man of God and that he knew the hidden things of hearts by the power of God, that is, he knew the hardness of his heart and his intention to kill King Benhadad in order to reign in his place, so that Hazael was ashamed, because his evil intentions had been exposed before Elisha.

8.10.1.en: After this Elisha wept, and Hazael was greatly astonished and afraid and wondered why the mighty man of God was weeping.

8.11.0.en: Hazael asked him the reason for his weeping, and he told him the reason: that by the spirit of prophecy he knew what would happen in days to come, and the evil that would befall Israel at the hands of Hazael, when he would burn their strongholds with fire, kill their soldiers with the sword, destroy their children and rip up their women with child.

8.11.1.en: Hazael pretended humility and submission to Elisha and denied that he would ever do harm to the children of Israel; he even described himself as contemptible, like a dog, and too insignificant to do these great evils. But in truth his heart was hard and selfish, loving itself and hating the people of God, though he feared Elisha the man of God.

8.11.2.en: Elisha went on with his warning to Hazael by telling him prophetically that he would become king over Aram and would use his authority and his army to commit these atrocities.

8.11.3.en: God's warnings come in succession and continually to caution you against evil, so do not treat them lightly and reject the word of God, but return to Him in repentance, and you will gain your soul.

8.12.0.en: Hazael returned from Elisha to the palace of his master Benhadad, who immediately asked him what Elisha had told him. He answered him briefly, saying that he would recover from his illness, and he did not tell him the rest of the prophecy, that he would die after his recovery. So Hazael was a liar, for half the truth is not the truth.

8.13.0.en: Thick cloth: a piece of wool used either as a cover or as a rug.

8.13.1.en: It appears that on the following day Benhadad began to recover and be healed of his illness, as Elisha had prophesied to him. Hazael felt that Benhadad would not die, so he advanced with brutality and treachery and took the thick cloth, dipped it in water and put it on the face of Benhadad, whose body was weak because of the illness, and stifled his breath, since a wet cloth prevents air from getting through. So Benhadad actually died. Then Hazael announced that the king had died, as though he had died of his illness, and set himself up as king over Aram. As a military commander with authority, he was able, by means of the soldiers loyal to him, to proclaim himself king.

8.13.3.en: 16- And in the fifth year of Joram the son of Ahab king of Israel, Jehoshaphat being then king of Judah, Jehoram the son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah began to reign. 17- Thirty and two years old was he when he began to reign; and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem. 18- And he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as did the house of Ahab: for the daughter of Ahab was his wife: and he did evil in the sight of the LORD. 19- Yet the LORD would not destroy Judah for David his servant's sake, as he promised him to give him alway a light, and to his children. 20- In his days Edom revolted from under the hand of Judah, and made a king over themselves. 21- So Joram went over to Zair, and all the chariots with him: and he rose by night, and smote the Edomites which compassed him about, and the captains of the chariots: and the people fled into their tents. 22- Yet Edom revolted from under the hand of Judah unto this day. Then Libnah revolted at the same time. 23- And the rest of the acts of Joram, and all that he did, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah? 24- And Joram slept with his fathers, and was buried with his fathers in the city of David: and Ahaziah his son reigned in his stead.

8.13.4.en: Note: These nine verses, 16-24, are a brief description of the period of the reign of Jehoram king of Judah. A fuller account of this king's reign is found in the whole of 2 Chronicles chapter 21, that is, verses 1 to 20.

8.14.0.en: It is noticed that Jehoram king of Judah began to reign in the fifth year of King Joram (Jehoram) king of Israel. But in this book (ch. 1:17) it tells us that Joram king of Israel began to reign in the second year of Jehoram king of Judah. The explanation of this apparent contradiction is that King Jehoshaphat, the father of Jehoram king of Judah, when he went out to war with Ahab to recover Ramoth Gilead from the Arameans, gave his son Jehoram the regency over the kingdom, because he did not know whether he would return alive or not; and when he returned alive, he reigned together with his son Jehoram. Two years after Jehoram was set up as king over Judah with his father, Joram began to reign over the kingdom of Israel, and five years after his reign began, Jehoshaphat gave the whole kingdom, that is, the full regency, to his son Jehoram, so that he became sole king over the kingdom. This means that he reigned fully five years after the reign of Joram king of Israel.

8.14.1.en: This means that Jehoram king of Judah reigned seven years with his father, and then received the kingdom alone, while Jehoshaphat was still alive at that time.

8.14.2.en: The similarity of names among the kings is because Jehoram king of Judah married the daughter of Ahab. There was a relationship between Jehoshaphat and Ahab, and as a political courtesy they gave their sons the same names. Jehoram king of Judah also named his son Ahaziah, who is the second son who reigned before Jehoram king of Israel, and he is the maternal uncle of Ahaziah king of Judah. The genealogy of the kings of Judah and Israel in this period:

8.14.3.en: Jehoshaphat, Ahab, Jehoram (husband of Athaliah), Ahaziah, Jehoram, Athaliah, who is ascribed to Omri her grandfather (v. 26), Ahaziah

8.15.0.en: Jehoram king of Judah was thirty-two years old when he began to reign alone, and his reign lasted eight years. The capital of his kingdom was Jerusalem.

8.16.0.en: King Jehoram walked in evil, that is, the worship of idols and evil lusts, like the kings of Israel, the most evil of whom were King Ahab and his wicked wife Jezebel, because the wife of Jehoram king of Judah was Athaliah, the daughter of Ahab, and she influenced him and made him walk in evil.

8.16.1.en: Jehoshaphat thought that by allying himself with Ahab king of Israel he would grow stronger, but unfortunately he grew weak, because of the lack of God's blessing on him and the corruption of his descendants, due to their intermarriage with the house of Ahab. Strength is in a relationship with God and not with the wicked.

8.16.2.en: Examine your personal relationships carefully, the most important of which is marriage, followed by friends, for they certainly influence you. These persons should have a relationship with God, so that they help you in your spiritual life; otherwise their company is bad company, which corrupts your life and leads you away from God.

8.17.0.en: In spite of the very great evil of Jehoram king of Judah, God did not destroy the kingdom of Judah, who had angered Him, for the sake of the great David, because He had promised him to keep his descendants as kings over the kingdom forever. So He was long-suffering toward Jehoram and toward all the kings of Judah, until Christ came from them, who reigns forever.

8.17.1.en: God's keeping a light in the kingdom of Judah means the continuation of the kingship for the descendants of David; for the presence of a light in a house means that there are inhabitants in it, and the putting out of the light means that there are no inhabitants, that is, that the house is abandoned.

8.17.2.en: God is long-suffering toward you at many times, not because of your righteousness, for your evils provoke Him, but because of the many prayers that are offered for you and because of the righteous to whom you are related. In this He gives you an opportunity to repent, so do not be negligent and lose the opportunity.

8.18.0.en: Zair: it is Seir, the chain of mountains where the Edomites live.

8.18.1.en: A rebellion arose from the Edomites against those living south of Judah, so Jehoram king of Judah went out with soldiers and war chariots to subdue them, and he was able to defeat them. But afterward a company of Edomite soldiers surrounded him to destroy him, yet he was able to break through it and return to Jerusalem, and the soldiers of the kingdom of Judah fled, each to his tent, when they found their king surrounded by this Edomite company. That is, Jehoram first triumphed over Edom, but he nearly perished when they surrounded him, and he was able to escape, and the soldiers of Judah also fled. It is noted that the text of this verse is very brief, so we have given this detailed explanation.

8.19.0.en: Libnah: a city in Judah located southwest of Jerusalem.

8.19.1.en: From the days of Jehoram, Edom rebelled against the kingdom of Judah and set up a king for themselves, and they remained in this rebellion until near the first century before Christ, when the Maccabees subdued them.

8.19.2.en: The revolt of Edom is the fulfillment of Isaac's prophecy to his son Esau, when he told him that he would be subject to the descendants of Jacob, but a time would come when he would break Jacob's yoke and rebel against him.

8.19.3.en: Because of the evil of Jehoram king of Judah, the city of Libnah rebelled against him; it is a city in Judah in which priests lived, who could not bear his evils, so they rebelled against him at the same time as the rebellion of Edom, and perhaps other cities of Judah rebelled against Jehoram. God allowed these rebellions, in the hope that he would take heed and turn back from his evil, but unfortunately he continued in it.

8.19.4.en: The phrase "unto this day" means: to the day this book was written.

8.20.0.en: The rest of the deeds that Jehoram did are recorded in "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah," a book the Jews had for recording the events of the kings of Judah, which is different from the Chronicles recorded in the Holy Bible.

8.21.0.en: Jehoram died and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and his son Ahaziah inherited the throne. Because of Jehoram's evil, he was not buried in the tombs of the kings, but only in the city of David.

8.21.2.en: 25- In the twelfth year of Joram the son of Ahab king of Israel did Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah begin to reign.

8.21.3.en: 26- Two and twenty years old was Ahaziah when he began to reign; and he reigned one year in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Athaliah, the daughter of Omri king of Israel. 27- And he walked in the way of the house of Ahab, and did evil in the sight of the LORD, as did the house of Ahab: for he was the son in law of the house of Ahab. 28- And he went with Joram the son of Ahab to the war against Hazael king of Syria in Ramothgilead; and the Syrians wounded Joram. 29- And king Joram went back to be healed in Jezreel of the wounds which the Syrians had given him at Ramah, when he fought against Hazael king of Syria. And Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah went down to see Joram the son of Ahab in Jezreel, because he was sick.

8.21.4.en: The story of Ahaziah is repeated in 2 Chronicles ch. 22, verses 1-9, and verses 1-6 agree with what is in 2 Kings, and 2 Chronicles adds in verses

8.21.5.en: 7-9 some events of the end of Ahaziah's life that 2 Kings does not mention.

8.22.0.en: Ahaziah: he is called Jehoahaz in (2 Chr 21:17) and also called Azariah in (2 Chr 22:

8.22.1.en: 6). After the death of Jehoram king of Judah, his son Ahaziah reigned over Judah, and it was then the twelfth year of Jehoram king of Israel. Although (ch. 9:29) mentions that Ahaziah king of Judah began to reign in the eleventh year of Jehoram king of Israel, that is because parts of a year are counted as a year; in this chapter they were counted, so it became twelve years, whereas in (ch. 9) they were not counted.

8.23.0.en: Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he became king, and his reign was very short, for he reigned one year in Jerusalem. His mother was Athaliah, the daughter of Ahab, the son of Omri king of Israel. Here is a pause for comparison between the mother and grandmother who were the secret of blessing in the life of Timothy (2 Tim 1:5), and the mother Athaliah and the grandmother Jezebel, who were the secret of misery and corruption in the life of Ahaziah.

8.24.0.en: King Ahaziah walked in evil, that is, he worshiped idols and encouraged his people to do so. This was because his mother Athaliah was the daughter of Ahab, the most wicked of the kings of Israel, who led them in the worship of idols, so Ahaziah the grandson continued in the way of his grandfather Ahab, that is, in the way of evil.

8.24.1.en: The meaning of the name Athaliah is "whom Jehovah afflicts," and the meaning of the name Joram, Athaliah's brother, is "whom Jehovah exalts" or "supports." We notice from this that the wicked Ahab used the name of Jehovah in naming his children, but sometimes for good and sometimes for evil, for Ahab halted between two opinions, sometimes being with God and sometimes against Him, since Ahab worshiped idols. So his children and grandchildren became like him in evil, drawing near to God at times and then departing from Him. This of course angers God greatly and brings His wrath upon them.

8.24.2.en: Be obedient to your parents, but in what agrees with God. If they walk in evil, do not follow them, for God must be obeyed more than men; indeed, by holding fast to God you may be able to draw them to Him, in proportion to your humility and your prayers.

8.25.0.en: Ahaziah king of Judah helped Joram king of Israel and went out with him to fight Hazael king of Aram. This was because Joram king of Israel was Ahaziah's maternal uncle, the brother of Athaliah his mother, and both walked in evil like Ahab. The cause of the war was Joram's attempt to recover the city of Ramoth Gilead. He was able to recover it from Hazael, as is proved by the anointing of Jehu as king while he was in it (ch. 9:1-15), who was the king after Joram king of Israel, but Joram was struck and wounded in the war.

8.26.0.en: After the war with Hazael ended, Joram king of Israel went to Jezreel, a place where the kings spent the summer, that is, a beautiful place where Joram spent a period to be healed of the wounds he had received in the war with the Arameans. Ahaziah returned with his army to Jerusalem, then went down from Jerusalem, which is in the mountains, to Jezreel, which is in the valley, to ask after and care for the condition of his uncle Joram king of Israel. Jehu reigns and the house of Ahab is slain
